name: Wei Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm one of five at a studio on the ring road, next to a tyre place. Most of our clients are estate agents and car dealers, so my day is property brochures, 'for sale' boards, and web banners saying zero percent finance. This morning I was swapping grey skies for blue ones on twelve house photos. I'm on the phone a lot too, because the dealers always want it by Friday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I actually like the clients. The car guys are funny and they're straight with you. What wears me out is that it's the same brochure fifty times with a different kitchen. And the money is thin: I rent a room in a shared house and I've got maybe two weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hype was oversold, like most things. Some tools are handy, like the sky replacement, and the rest is noise. I'd say that at work and leave it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not that comfortable anyway. One of our estate agents was bought by a national chain this summer, and the chain has its own designers. My boss Graham has frozen pay for this year, so I'm already behind on everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the work and using the odd tool to speed up photo edits. I'd ask the car dealers whether they'd want video ads, because I could learn that. And I'd start looking at jobs in the city, which is an hour away, just to see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. Not because of AI. Because of the pay freeze and the clients we're losing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen if another estate agent got bought?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd lose maybe a quarter of our work. Graham would have to let someone go, and I'm the most recent hire after Jas. It's a small town, there's nowhere else to walk into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving to the city be realistic on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not straight away. The deposit for a room there is more than I've got. I'd need a job lined up first, and probably a month of commuting on the train.

say: I'd say the hype was **oversold**, with a few **handy tools**.
I'd say that at work and **leave it** there.
think: An estate agent client was **bought by a chain** with its own designers.
Graham (my boss) has **frozen pay**, so I'm already behind.
do: Keep using the odd tool to speed up **photo edits**.
Look at jobs in the **city**, an hour away.
feel: **Anxious** about the **pay freeze** and lost clients, not AI.

fieldNote: Wei's worry in the mildest picture is **client loss** and a pay freeze.
He's the **second-newest** hire, which he sees as making him vulnerable.
Moving to the city is blocked by the **deposit** on a room.

steps.text: Pitch video ads to the car dealers this spring
Use the sky-replacement tool to speed up property photo edits
Browse design jobs in the city an hour away

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we should be sensible about it, not scared. Learn what works, drop what doesn't. That's what I'd tell my mates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, our clients are exactly the kind who'll just do it themselves. A car dealer with an app can make a finance banner in two minutes. So the studio shrinks, and my role probably goes or turns into checking what the app made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd spend the first month learning the tools properly, the ones the other studios use, once I see they work. I'd talk to the dealers about moving onto their marketing team, because they like me. And I'd stop eating out and get the cheaper phone plan, maybe fifty a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like watching the client list get shorter every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the dealers like you. Is that a real job offer or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A hope, for now. The manager at the Ford dealer once joked about poaching me. I'd go and have a coffee with him and find out if it was a joke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm fine, which they'd half believe. My dad would tell me to get into sales because sales always pays. He's probably right, annoyingly.

say: I'd say it's a **big change** and we should be **sensible**, not scared.
I'd tell my mates to learn what works and **drop** what doesn't.
think: Our clients are exactly the kind who'll **do it themselves**.
My role probably goes or turns into **checking** what the app made.
do: Learn the tools **properly** once I see they work.
Ask the **Ford dealer** about joining their marketing team.
Save about **fifty a month** by cutting eating out.

fieldNote: Wei's **clients** are the ones most likely to do design themselves.
He'd jump **sideways** to a client's marketing team rather than retrain.
His dad's advice about **sales** keeps coming back to him.

steps.text: Learn the AI design tools other studios already use
Have coffee with the Ford dealer's manager about a marketing job
Stop eating out and switch to a cheaper phone plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to stay calm and the government needs a plan, quickly. I'm not a protest person. I'd just want someone sensible in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm gone within a year. My whole job is screen work, so it goes on the AGI date with no delay. The dealers wouldn't need a marketing person either, because the AI would do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to my dad and ask about selling cars, actually standing on the forecourt. People still want to shake a hand when they buy a car. I'd give up my room and move back to my parents' to stop the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd wasted the degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling cars is quite a shift. What does it mean that robots come about three years later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling isn't really a robot thing anyway, it's talking. But if AI can talk to customers better than me, I'm not sure. I'd have maybe three to five years before even that thins out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you feel moving back home at twenty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassed, but there'd be a lot of us doing it. My mum would be pleased, honestly. My dad would make me pay something, which is fair.

say: I'd say we should stay **calm** and the **government** needs a plan.
I'm not a **protest** person; I'd just want someone sensible in charge.
think: I'm **gone** within a year, because it's all **screen work**.
The dealers wouldn't need a **marketing person** either.
do: Ask my dad about **selling cars** on a forecourt.
Give up my room and move **back home**.
Pay my parents a **fair share** for keep.
S2.quote: People still want to shake a hand when they buy a car.
fieldNote: Wei moves to **sales**, following his dad's long-standing advice.
He sees **talking to people** as his last edge, but doubts it lasts.
Moving **home** is embarrassing but practical for him.

steps.text: Ask his dad to help him get a car sales job
Give up the rented room and move back to his parents'
Pay his parents a small amount for keep while he resets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, if people start now. I'd tell friends to look at what can't be done from a screen. That's the sensible line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, design is a job I'd do for three or four more years, not a career. That's hard to say out loud at twenty-seven. But I'd rather plan for it than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd ask the Ford dealer for weekend sales shifts to see if I'm any good at it. I'd keep the studio job during the week. I'd also save a hundred a month from the extra money, so I've got a cushion when I switch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed still, but with a plan. It's less of a drop and more of a staircase.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in 2031, when AGI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling cars full time, I hope. And maybe using the AI myself to do the dealer's ads, since I'd know how they should look. That's a nice little extra.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2034, when robots come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot doesn't sell cars, but a website might. I'd be thirty-five and might have to change again. I'd want some savings by then.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** if people **start now**.
I'd tell friends to look at what can't be done from a **screen**.
think: Design is a job for **three or four** more years, not a career.
That's **hard to say** out loud at twenty-seven.
do: Work **weekend sales** shifts at the Ford dealer.
Keep the **studio job** during the week.
Save **a hundred a month** from the extra money.
feel: **Alarmed**, but with a plan like a **staircase** instead of a drop.
S3.quote: Design is a job I'd do for three or four more years, not a career. That's hard to say out loud at twenty-seven.
fieldNote: Wei **tests** sales part-time before leaving design, true to his steady nature.
He'd use AI on the side to make **dealer ads**, mixing old and new skills.

steps.text: Work weekend sales shifts at the Ford dealer
Save a hundred a month from the weekend pay
Make the dealer's ads with AI tools for extra money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway and there's no need to panic. Learn the tools, keep an eye on it. That's the sensible thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could stay in design a while longer and still move in time. I'd want to be in a client-facing role by thirty-two or so. I'm good with people, so that's my bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd learn the AI tools well, so the studio sees me as useful. I'd ask Graham to let me handle more client calls, so I build that side. And I'd try to save a month of rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but a slow kind. Like knowing your car will need a new clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a client-facing role. Inside design or outside it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Inside, first. An account manager, the person who deals with the client. If that goes too, then sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably I'd move to the city in a year or two, where there are more studios. With two years of warning I'd move home. With ten years, I'd go where the work is.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway** with no need to panic.
I'd tell people to **learn the tools** and keep watching.
think: I could stay in design longer and still **move in time**.
I'd want a **client-facing** role by about thirty-two.
do: Learn the AI tools **well** this year.
feel: Slowly **anxious**, like a car that will need a **new clutch**.
S4.quote: With two years of warning I'd move home. With ten years, I'd go where the work is.
fieldNote: Ten years shifts Wei towards **account management** inside design first.
He'd move to the **city** with a decade, but **home** with two years.
His anxiety is **slow** and practical, not frantic.

steps.text: Learn the studio's AI tools well this year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Two years isn't enough to switch, and I'd end up at my parents' with a degree I can't use. What would help is cheap or free short courses, and maybe a bit of help with rent while you change.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how small the town is. In a city, you'd lose one studio job and find another. Here, there's two studios and a print works, and that's it.

headlineQuote: In a city, you'd lose one studio job and find another. Here, there's two studios and a print works, and that's it.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old designer** at a studio serving **estate agents** and car dealers.
He uses AI **now and then**, mostly for property photo edits.
He's pragmatic and calm in public, and leans on his dad's advice about **sales**.
Across the pictures, he moves from design towards **client-facing** work, then car sales.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years isn't enough to **switch**.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap or free **short courses** and some help with **rent**.
